svg.title: Where a blast-radius guard belongs, and the three guards this server applies
svg.desc: Two lanes compare where the same limit can be enforced, drawn on one four-column grid so the steps line up. The upper lane, crossed, puts the guard inside the tool body, and the change reaches a person before it is checked: propose five hundred, ask the human, the human approves, and only then does the tool refuse anyway, so somebody authorized a change the server was never going to make and learned that prompts do not mean anything. The lower lane, ticked, puts the guard inside the resolver, which the software development kit runs before it renders the question: propose five hundred, guard_replicas runs in the column the upper lane spent on asking a person, the call fails with an error the model can read, and the ask-the-human box in the last column is struck through because it is never reached. A note records that the test asserts both an empty question list and an empty list of recorded cluster calls. Below the lanes, a table gives the three guards, their defaults and the environment variable that changes each: a maximum replica count of twenty, three protected namespaces closed to writes, and per-call ceilings of five hundred log lines and forty thousand log bytes. Two closing lines state that reads are never restricted, because refusing to restart a pod in kube-system is not a reason to refuse to look at one, and that these guards are convenience rather than security, since they live in the same process as the next bug while the control that matters is role-based access control on the service account.
svg.text: Guards fire before the human, not after
The same limit, in two places. Only one of them keeps a person from approving the impossible.
the change reaches a person before it is checked
A person authorized something the server was never going to do, and learned that prompts do not mean anything.
the SDK runs the resolver before it renders the question
assert seen == [] and assert fake.recorder.names() == []: no question was rendered, and no API call was made.
Log lines and bytes per call
Reads are never restricted. Refusing to restart a pod in kube-system is not a reason to refuse to look at one.
These guards are convenience, not security: they live in the same process as the next bug. The control that matters is RBAC on the service account.
